content: Observational data from multiple countries has revealed a low uptake of hepatitis D virus (HDV) testing when using a risk-based testing approach. However, a significant increase in case detection has been observed with the implementation of universal testing strategies. These strategies involve laboratory-based reflex testing for anti-HDV antibodies in all individuals who test positive for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). The anticipated benefits of universal HDV testing, despite some uncertainties, are considered to outweigh potential harms. Key advantages include: 1. Universal HDV antibody testing among HBsAg-positive individuals is likely to improve testing uptake, facilitate early diagnosis, and enhance individuals' awareness of their HDV status and prognosis. This approach also supports linkage to preventive measures, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) monitoring, and future treatment options. 2. Promising results from novel HDV treatment options in clinical trials, including one drug approved by the European Medicines Agency (EMA), highlight the importance of identifying HDV-infected individuals. This identification enables the establishment of patient registries, which can streamline access to optimal care, monitoring, clinical trials, and effective treatments as they become available. 3. Universal HDV antibody testing can improve the availability and quality of epidemiological data and surveillance, which are critical for informing national testing strategies and public health responses. 4. A universal testing approach may drive demand for higher-quality diagnostics and foster competition. This could lead to the development of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for HDV antibodies and standardized commercial HDV RNA assays, facilitating decentralized care. Challenges associated with universal HDV antibody testing include: 1. Universal testing is initially more expensive than risk-based approaches, as it involves automatic screening of numerous samples, particularly in countries with high hepatitis B prevalence. 2. Implementing universal reflex HDV antibody testing is challenging in lowand middle-income countries, where HBsAg testing is often conducted using RDTs in clinics or community settings. Limited laboratory capacity for anti-HDV antibody testing further complicates implementation. An alternative approach could involve collecting additional samples from individuals with positive HBsAg RDT results and sending them to central laboratories with the necessary testing capacity. 3. Substantial increases in diagnostic laboratory capacity and resources are required for universal HDV antibody testing, which may be difficult to achieve in lowand middle-income countries in the near future. 4. Individuals who test positive for anti-HDV antibodies will still require additional HDV RNA testing to confirm active (viraemic) infection and subsequent linkage to care and treatment. 5. Limited availability of effective and affordable HDV treatment options means that many individuals identified as positive for both anti-HDV antibodies and HDV RNA may not initially receive treatment. This presents an ethical challenge, necessitating thorough preand post-test counseling. However, individuals diagnosed with HDV infection will be prioritized for more frequent monitoring, including HCC screening. The current patchy implementation of risk-based HDV testing has contributed to low overall testing and diagnosis rates. Effective risk-based testing requires healthcare providers to have knowledge of national and local HDV prevalence and high-risk groups. However, limited awareness among healthcare providers and incomplete global epidemiological data on HDV infection further hinder the effectiveness of this approach. Additional barriers include stigma, limited access to testing, variable diagnostic performance of HDV assays, and the lack of highly effective and well-tolerated treatment options. Universal HDV antibody testing promotes equity in access to testing across populations and facilities without requiring information about risk groups or high-risk behaviors. However, this depends on widespread access to HBsAg testing as a foundation for universal HDV testing. High-risk groups, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, may face challenges in accessing HBV testing services and, consequently, HDV testing. Although no formal cost-effectiveness analyses have compared universal and risk-based screening, universal HDV antibody testing will require increased resources to test all HBsAg-positive samples. Existing studies have shown a substantial increase in identified cases with universal testing. However, uncertainties remain regarding the costs associated with tests and additional service delivery, which vary by epidemiology, setting, and country. Treatment costs for identified cases will also evolve as new treatment options and associated monitoring requirements become available. Several professional society guidelines now recommend universal HDV testing for HBsAg-positive individuals, with retesting advised when clinically indicated, such as during aminotransferase flares or acute decompensation of chronic liver disease. Laboratory-based reflex anti-HDV testing has been implemented in multiple hospitals across Europe and other regions. The recommended testing strategy for diagnosing HDV infection in HBsAg-positive individuals involves serological screening for total anti-HDV antibodies, followed by molecular testing for HDV RNA to confirm active infection. Reflex testing for anti-HDV antibodies and HDV RNA may be considered where feasible. Assays should meet minimum quality, safety, and performance standards, with HDV RNA testing harmonized to WHO standards and results reported in IU/mL. Primers targeting the conserved ribozyme region of the HDV genome are recommended for genotype inclusivity, as certain genotypes are suboptimally detected in sub-Saharan Africa. Serological testing followed by PCR RNA assessment is the standard method for diagnosing HDV infection. While data on diagnostic accuracy are limited, available anti-HDV and HDV RNA assays have demonstrated satisfactory performance. All anti-HDV-positive results should be followed by HDV RNA measurement to confirm viraemic infection, minimizing the implications of false-positive serology. Adequate counseling and education on test interpretation and linkage to care are essential. Currently, all available anti-HDV and HDV RNA assays are laboratory-based, requiring specialized equipment and specimen handling. There are no point-of-care (POC) assays for HDV RNA, and existing assays may underestimate or fail to detect certain HDV genotypes, particularly those native to the WHO African Region. Standardized testing strategies are crucial for ensuring high-quality care and optimal resource use.
